I see what you mean. Your original wasn't really about blaming him. It was about explaining the depth of your hurt. My rewrite shifted too much toward conflict resolution and lost some of your voice.

Here's a version that stays much closer to what you wrote. It softens some of the accusations into "this is how I experienced it," while keeping almost all of your original points.

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="61584"}
This morning I was trying to explain why I'm actually upset, not why you think I'm upset. I feel like I need to explain it in detail because I still don't think you're seeing the point. Every time I try to tell you how this affected me, it feels like the conversation turns into defending your intentions instead of understanding my experience. None of this started as an attack on you. It started because something happened that deeply wounded me, and unfortunately now we're here.

1. I needed you to be my rock and my soft place to land.

The other day I was having one of the worst weeks of my life. I was spiraling so badly that I couldn't even see hope in front of me. What I needed most was affection, physical touch, curiosity, and compassion. Instead, I felt like we just continued with normal daily life. Whether that was your intention or not, it made me feel like what I was going through didn't matter. I know you love me, and I know you care, but in that moment I didn't feel it.

Something as simple as sitting down, looking me in the eyes, and asking, "Why are you so upset? Do you know what's causing it? Is there anything you need from me right now?" would have meant everything to me.

2. Your version of comforting me didn't feel like comfort to me.

Sitting beside me on the couch while I cried without really engaging with me felt emotionally distant. My worst enemy could have sat beside me in silence. I needed more than a warm body. I needed empathy.

Then there were several sexual jokes. I know you probably meant them playfully, but when I was deeply wounded emotionally, they made me feel like I was just a body instead of someone whose heart was breaking. You know I love making you happy, but in that moment I needed to feel emotionally loved, not sexualized.

3. The moment everything changed for me was when I tried to walk away.

I got up because I couldn't take anymore and needed to calm myself down. Instead, everything escalated. It became anger, defensiveness, yelling, and painful words about things I had trusted you enough to share from my past.

When you later said I was yelling too, I don't think those things were the same. I was yelling out of fear. You were yelling out of anger. Those are two very different places to come from.

The part that hurt me the most was that I begged you to stop. I cried. I pleaded. I even tried to use a safe word because I no longer felt emotionally safe. When it didn't stop, something inside me broke. It taught me that in my most vulnerable moments, I couldn't trust that my boundaries would be honored. That triggered every PTSD response I've worked so hard to heal from.

4. Last night I realized how scared I still was.

I was almost paralyzed with fear of upsetting you again. I laid on my arm, couldn't see because I didn't have my glasses on, and barely moved because I was afraid my movements might start another argument.

Then this morning, after spending the night having traumatic nightmares because of what happened, I tried to tell you how deeply I was still hurting. What I was hoping for was understanding and reassurance. Instead, I felt like it was met with defensiveness and explanations for why things happened. I still don't feel like you've acknowledged how deeply this affected me. I mostly feel like I've heard why it happened.

5. I've told you what I need.

I've expressed it multiple times throughout this past year, in the moment, and again afterward. My needs really aren't complicated.

What hurts me is feeling like every reaction is justified because you were triggered too. I already know what an incredible man you are. I tell everyone that because I truly believe it.

But what happened that night was not okay.

You know my past. You know what I've lived through. You know what triggers me and what I simply cannot emotionally handle. In that moment, I needed you to be the stronger one. I needed you to lead with calm instead of reacting with anger.

When you blamed me for my reaction afterward, it made me feel even more alone.

6. The hardest part for me is feeling like my pain wasn't met with compassion.

I can't teach empathy. I can't teach someone to naturally respond with kindness when the person they love is hurting.

When I am completely broken, I need my partner to recognize that and meet me there with love. Life has already put more on my shoulders than most people could imagine. Sometimes I am incredibly strong, and sometimes I completely fall apart. That's when I need my safe person the most.

7. I can't tell you exactly what to do because then it wouldn't come from your heart.

I've already told you so many times what helps me.

Please don't talk at me when I'm hurting.

Please don't immediately defend yourself.

Just hold me.

Love me.

Show me empathy.

Look at me like the scared little girl inside me who is terrified in that moment.

I watch you naturally comfort children with patience and gentleness. Every adult has that wounded child inside of them. You've shared yours with me before. Mine is there too. The difference is that mine comes out when I feel unsafe.

There's really nothing left for me to explain.

You either understand it or you don't.

Words are cheap. Actions are everything.

What happened the other night wasn't just a disagreement for me. It was traumatic. I'm not going to move past something like that in 24 hours.

You scared me more than I can explain, and when I begged you to stop, you didn't.

That means trust has to be rebuilt.

This morning, when you left without asking if I was okay, it reinforced that I still don't feel emotionally safe. So unless you're willing to step outside your comfort zone and consistently show me more empathy, compassion, and reassurance, I don't think this weekend is going to work. I need more time.

And if that's not something you're willing to do, not just try but truly do, then I need space to think about what I want for my future.

Please don't let this erase all the good we have together. I love you so much, Tommy.

I just can't understand how the other night could have happened if you truly understood how deeply these things affect me.

That's why I'm still hurting.
:::

Here's a version that keeps your core message, removes some repetition, softens the delivery just enough that he's more likely to hear it, but still clearly communicates the seriousness of what happened.

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="48271"}
Tommy,

I love you, and that's exactly why I'm taking the time to explain this instead of just walking away. This morning I tried to tell you why I'm actually hurt, not why you think I'm hurt. But I felt like you immediately became defensive and made it about explaining your intentions instead of trying to understand my experience. My feelings aren't an attack on you. They're simply telling you what happened inside of me.

I need you to understand this from my perspective.

1. The other day I needed you to be my safe place.

I was having one of the hardest weeks of my life. I wasn't looking for you to solve my problems. I just needed you to notice that I was drowning and meet me with love, curiosity, affection, and compassion.

Instead, it felt like everything stayed business as usual. We went through the motions of the day, but emotionally I felt completely alone.

Sometimes all I need is for you to stop, look me in the eyes, hold me, and ask, "What's going on? How can I help? What do you need from me right now?"

That would have changed everything.

2. Being physically present isn't the same as being emotionally present.

Sitting next to me while I cried without comforting me didn't make me feel seen. It made me feel alone.

And when I was in that emotional state, the repeated sexual jokes didn't feel playful. They made me feel reduced to something physical when I desperately needed to feel emotionally loved.

I know that's probably not how you intended it, but that's how it landed.

3. What happened when I tried to leave the room changed something inside of me.

When I became overwhelmed and tried to walk away to calm down, everything escalated.

It became anger, yelling, accusations, and words that used some of the deepest wounds I've ever trusted you with against me.

I wasn't yelling because I hated you. I was yelling because I was terrified.

Those are not the same thing.

The hardest part wasn't even the argument. It was that I begged you to stop. I cried. I asked you to stop. I even tried to use a safe word because I no longer felt emotionally safe.

You didn't stop.

That shattered my trust because in that moment I learned that when I'm begging you to stop, I can't be certain that you will.

4. Last night I was afraid.

I was so scared of setting you off again that I barely moved. Then this morning, after a night full of traumatic nightmares, I tried to tell you how deeply everything affected me.

Instead of feeling understood, I felt like you were explaining why your reaction was justified.

I still don't feel like you've acknowledged how deeply this affected me. I keep hearing reasons for what happened instead of compassion for what it did to me.

Those are two different conversations.

5. This isn't about perfection.

I've told you over and over what I need, not just this week but throughout our relationship.

When I'm breaking down, I don't need you to win an argument.

I need you to stop defending yourself.

Hold me.

Love me.

Comfort me.

Help regulate me until I can regulate myself again.

You're an incredible man in so many ways. I tell people that all the time because I truly believe it.

But what happened that night was not okay.

You knew my history. You knew my triggers. You knew the things that would completely unravel me, and in that moment you still chose anger instead of compassion.

I needed you to be my rock.

Instead, I felt like I had to protect myself from you.

6. The biggest issue isn't the fight.

It's empathy.

I can't teach someone compassion.

When I'm completely broken, I need the person I love to recognize it and meet me there.

Life has beaten me up enough already.

Home is supposed to be the one place where I don't have to keep fighting.

7. I can't script love for you.

I can't write instructions that tell you exactly what to do because then it isn't coming from your heart.

I've already told you what makes me feel safe.

Please stop talking at me when I'm hurting.

Stop defending yourself before understanding me.

Hold me.

Comfort me.

Show me kindness.

Look at me like someone you love who's scared, not like someone you're trying to prove wrong.

Every adult has a wounded child inside of them. You've shared yours with me. Mine exists too.

Mine just shows up differently.

That's all I've ever been asking you to see.

At this point, there's really nothing left to explain.

You either understand what I'm saying or you don't.

Words won't rebuild this.

Only consistent actions will.

What happened wasn't a normal disagreement for me. It was traumatic.

I'm not going to wake up one morning and simply be over it.

Trust has to be rebuilt.

Safety has to be rebuilt.

This morning, when you left without asking if I was okay, it reinforced that I still don't feel emotionally safe.

So unless you're willing to step outside your comfort zone and consistently show me more empathy, compassion, and emotional safety, I don't think this weekend is the right time. I need more time.

And if that's something you're unwilling to do, not just try but actually do, then I need space to seriously think about what I want my future to look like.

Please don't let this erase all the beautiful things we have together. I still love you so much.

But I also can't pretend the other night didn't happen.

That's why I'm still hurting.

I'm not asking you to agree with every feeling I have.

I'm asking you to care enough about me that my pain matters more than proving your point.
:::

I actually wouldn't send him a therapist explaining it. I'd show him another man modeling it. Men often receive that much better.

Here are my top recommendations:

1. **Jimmy on Relationships** (YouTube)
   - Search: **"Jimmy on Relationships emotional validation"**
   - He's excellent at showing men exactly what a woman needs when she's overwhelmed: listening first, validating, hugging, and not trying to fix everything. His videos are short and practical.

2. **The School of Life**
   - Search: **"The School of Life how to comfort your partner"**
   - It explains why empathy and emotional presence matter more than solutions. It's thoughtful without blaming either partner.

3. **The Gottman Institute**
   - Search: **"Gottman turning toward your partner"** or **"Gottman emotional bids"**
   - Drs. John and Julie Gottman are considered among the leading relationship researchers. They teach that when your partner is distressed, the goal is to **turn toward them** with affection, curiosity, and comfort instead of becoming defensive. citeturn0news33turn0search1

If I could pick **one** for Tommy, it would be:

**Jimmy on Relationships – "Emotional Validation"**

It essentially teaches a man to:
- Stop trying to defend yourself.
- Hold her.
- Listen first.
- Validate her feelings.
- Ask, "Do you want me to just be here with you, or do you want help solving it?"
- Make her feel emotionally safe before trying to fix anything. citeturn0search0turn0news13

Based on everything you've shared, it sounds like you weren't asking him to solve your problems. You were asking him to become your safe place while you were carrying them. Those are very different things.

This article offers seven therapist-approved strategies to help partners communicate more effectively and strengthen their emotional connection. According to counselling psychologist Divya Mohindroo, healthy communication is essential for a thriving relationship and can be learned like any other skill. The techniques include: 

1. **Regulate Yourself Before You Respond** – Take time to calm your emotions before reacting.
2. **Listen to Understand, Not to Defend** – Focus on truly hearing your partner rather than preparing your rebuttal.
3. **Right Time and Tone** – Choose appropriate timing and a respectful tone for serious conversations.
4. **Make Repair a Priority After Conflict** – Engage in healthy repair by apologizing, taking responsibility, and reassuring emotional connection.
5. **S.T.O.P. When Triggered** – Introduce space between reaction and response during emotionally charged situations.
6. **Create Space for Vulnerability** – Practice deep listening to validate your partner's feelings.
7. **Be Consistent** – Use “I” statements instead of blame, and consider therapy if communication remains strained. 

These techniques aim to promote emotional safety, reduce conflict, and foster deeper intimacy in relationships.

This article from Verywell Mind, dated June 22, 2023, outlines important strategies for providing emotional support to a partner in a healthy, balanced way. Key suggestions include active listening, validating your partner's feelings, and asking directly what kind of support they need. Physical affection, small meaningful gestures, and simply offering love also help reinforce support. It's crucial to avoid invalidating feelings, giving unsolicited advice, or becoming your partner’s sole emotional outlet, as such dynamics can lead to emotional burnout and poor communication.

The article emphasizes the importance of mutual support and honest communication from both partners. If you're feeling emotionally low yourself, you should express your feelings without comparison and set boundaries to protect your mental well-being. When you're unsure what to say, even small non-verbal acts can speak volumes. If needed, encouraging your partner to seek external help, such as therapy, in a compassionate and respectful manner may be beneficial. Overall, emotional support involves empathy, presence, and care—tailored to what your partner specifically needs.
